From SK hynix’s 2Q Earnings Call Q&A

Q. What is the status of HBM price negotiations for 2027? What is the pricing outlook and the status of contract discussions for HBM3, HBM4, and the upcoming HBM4E?

A. We are currently discussing 2027 HBM supply volumes and pricing with our major customers. Negotiations are proceeding smoothly, supported by robust customer demand. However, we ask for your understanding that we cannot disclose individual customers’ contract terms or pricing details at this time.

Given the recent sharp increase in conventional DRAM prices, these market conditions could also influence HBM price negotiations. However, HBM pricing is not determined solely by movements in conventional DRAM prices.

Compared with conventional DRAM, HBM requires substantially greater resources, including more wafers, advanced process technologies, TSV, packaging, and production capacity. With each new generation, customers’ performance and quality requirements become more demanding, while the development and qualification processes grow increasingly complex.

Accordingly, we negotiate prices individually with customers by comprehensively considering not only conventional DRAM pricing and supply-demand conditions, but also the resources required to produce HBM, opportunity costs, technological complexity, and the value our products provide to customers.

Our focus is on securing an appropriate level of profitability commensurate with the differentiated value we provide to customers, while supporting the healthy and sustainable growth of the AI ecosystem.

Building on our accumulated technological and cost competitiveness, stable mass-production capabilities, strong customer trust, and close collaboration, we will maintain solid profitability in our HBM business. Through product transitions and greater customer value creation, we aim to establish ourselves as a key partner capable of growing alongside our customers in the AI era.

Ultimately, we will continue to pursue sustainable long-term growth.
— Jukan (@jukan05) Jul 29, 2026

items.title: Samsung Electro-Mechanics to Raise MLCC Prices by 30% Starting August 1.
items.content:
Samsung Electro-Mechanics to Raise MLCC Prices by 30% Starting August 1.Jukan (@jukan05)Samsung Electro-Mechanics to Raise MLCC Prices

- Samsung Electro-Mechanics has sent customers a notice announcing that it plans to raise prices for certain MLCC products by 30% from August 1, 2026.

- The company explained that structural growth in global electronics demand has placed pressure on the supply chain beyond what it can absorb internally.

- Samsung Electro-Mechanics said that although it has continued to improve manufacturing efficiency and expand capacity, price adjustments for certain products have become unavoidable to maintain product quality and a stable supply.

- The price increase will apply to all MLCC products under Samsung Electro-Mechanics’ Markup Business Code, with the new prices taking effect for shipments made on or after August 1, 2026.

- The company emphasized that the price adjustment is unavoidable and said it will continue to supply high-quality products and support its customers’ businesses.

- Taiyo Yuden is also moving to raise MLCC prices from September 1, while noting that it may be unable to guarantee customers’ requested delivery schedules.

- Taiyo Yuden explained that it decided to adjust prices because ongoing increases in raw-material costs could no longer be absorbed through cost-cutting efforts alone.

- Even after the price adjustment, supply is expected to remain insufficient to fully meet demand, and the company may still be unable to guarantee on-time delivery.—  https://x.com/jukan05/status/2082240360085160357 
— Jukan (@jukan05) Jul 29, 2026

items.content:
>> TrendForce: Monthly Shipments by Korean and Japanese MLCC Makers Hit Record High on AI Demand; Spillover in Consumer Orders Becomes Visible

• According to TrendForce’s latest MLCC industry survey, strong AI demand drove Murata, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, and Taiyo Yuden—the three leading Korean and Japanese suppliers—to record their highest monthly shipment volumes in five years in June 2026. Meanwhile, continued spillover in consumer orders pushed up prices at other manufacturers and across distribution channels.

• As Korean and Japanese suppliers rapidly shift consumer-grade X5R capacity toward higher-spec X6S/X7R products for AI applications, capacity for mid- to high-capacitance consumer MLCCs (1µF–22µF) is coming under pressure. Inventory levels for key products have generally fallen to 30 days or less.

• Supply constraints have triggered a surge in urgent orders from distributors, agents, and Tier 2 and Tier 3 customers, further amplifying the order-spillover effect. As a result, order visibility at other manufacturers has improved markedly, accompanied by higher product prices. Distributors that had built inventories in advance have raised prices by an average of 20–25%, while spot-market prices have climbed to two to three times their previous levels. The consumer MLCC market is therefore exhibiting a structural divergence in which end demand remains weak while distribution-channel prices stay firm.
— Jukan (@jukan05) Jul 28, 2026

items.content:
TFHK Commentary: How Should We Understand the Current Correction in AI Hardware?

The market is always right. Changes in stock prices inevitably reflect the new variables the market is currently pricing in. Even as long-term bulls on the AI industry, we need to understand the core concerns driving this correction in AI semiconductor stocks.

The current market bears a striking resemblance to last autumn and winter. Following OpenAI’s large fundraising round, industry conditions were very strong, yet stocks continued to trade sideways. Market participants spent every day debating CapEx, ROI, valuations, and financing—much like they are doing now.

The conclusions from this quarter’s earnings reports remain overwhelmingly positive. GCP grew by 80%, the ROI of cloud investment was validated, Intel delivered a significant beat, and ASML, TSMC, and Intel raised their order or CapEx outlooks. Presumably, these companies also saw extremely strong downstream forecasts, giving even the most conservative players in the supply chain the confidence to make aggressive bets. Had this information emerged in May or June, semiconductor stocks would almost certainly have surged.

Now, however, every earnings release has instead become an opportunity for bears to reassess valuations and the long-term investment thesis. What we may be seeing is that the AI market is no longer in the “AI Summer” of May and June. The same positive developments now provide less support to share prices. Take GCP’s 80% growth as an example. Previously, the market’s first reaction would have been: “AI demand has exceeded expectations—the catalyst has arrived.” Now, the first response is: “So what? What about 2028? Can OpenAI become profitable? For how many more years can GPU prices keep rising? Margins are rising again, financing costs are increasing, and the entire CapEx thesis needs to be repriced.” In essence, the market has shifted from trading the growth of AI CapEx to trading its sustainability and ROI.

Market sentiment, as we perceive it, has already become extremely bearish. Even long-term bulls are beginning to question whether AI semiconductor stocks can continue to rise, and we are hearing almost no calls for new highs. When the market shifts from looking for further upside to searching for additional downside risks, it usually means that pessimistic expectations have already been largely priced in.

Nevertheless, we have no doubts about the fundamentals. We also believe that, ultimately, facts determine stock prices. So what would send these stocks higher again? Under the framework outlined above, additional capital-spending plans alone will no longer be enough to convince the bears. What is needed is validation of a new demand curve. The most powerful and direct catalyst would be the emergence of a blockbuster product. If “Coding 1.0” proved that AI can improve developer productivity, then “Coding 2.0” must demonstrate that AI agents can genuinely replace part of the software development process. Once new productivity use cases are validated, the market’s concerns about AI ROI may be redefined, and AI infrastructure spending will once again be viewed as “productivity investment” rather than a “cost.”
— Jukan (@jukan05) Jul 28, 2026

[Exclusive] SK hynix to Begin Mass Production of LPDDR6 in Second Half; Xiaomi to Be First Customer

SK hynix plans to begin mass-producing and shipping LPDDR6, its next-generation low-power mobile DRAM, in the second half of this year. Having completed development of the product in March, the company intends to make its first shipment to China’s Xiaomi for use in mobile devices. The launch is expected to further intensify competition among the three major memory manufacturers—Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, and Micron—in SOCAMM, a next-generation, LPDDR-based low-power memory module for AI servers.

According to industry sources on July 28, SK hynix will enter full-scale mass production of LPDDR6 in the second half of this year. Xiaomi is expected to be its first customer, with the memory slated for use in the company’s next-generation flagship smartphones. SK hynix’s LPDDR6 uses its sixth-generation 10nm-class (1c) process, offering improved data-transfer speeds and power efficiency over the previous generation.

In March, SK hynix announced that it had completed certification of what it described as the world’s first LPDDR6 product, saying, “We plan to complete preparations for mass production within the first half and begin supplying the product in the second half.” Regarding the reported Xiaomi deal, however, the company said it could not confirm information related to customers.

SK hynix began doing business with Xiaomi in 2013, supplying LPDDR3 for certain models, and is understood to have continued supplying mobile DRAM through the latest LPDDR5X generation.

Samsung Electronics and SK hynix currently lead the mobile DRAM market. Meanwhile, CXMT, China’s largest memory manufacturer, has been rapidly gaining ground following its stock-market debut, bringing its market share close to that of third-ranked U.S. chipmaker Micron. Samsung supplies LPDDR to Android smartphone manufacturers worldwide, while SK hynix has a strong position among Chinese smartphone brands.

The Xiaomi deal is expected to pave the way for SK hynix to expand LPDDR6 shipments to other Chinese smartphone manufacturers, including Vivo and Oppo. Chinese smartphone makers are increasingly adopting domestically produced memory from suppliers such as CXMT in their entry-level lineups, but their flagship models—which require higher performance—remain dependent on LPDDR from the three major global memory manufacturers.

LPDDR is primarily used in mobile devices such as smartphones and tablet PCs. By reducing power consumption while maintaining high performance, it has recently experienced explosive demand from AI servers. Some industry observers expect it to become a major growth driver for the memory market after HBM, or high-bandwidth memory.

LPDDR supply prices have recently risen to levels comparable with those of DRAM, whose prices have been soaring. The increase stems from supply bottlenecks caused by memory manufacturers concentrating their production capacity on commodity DRAM and HBM.

As LPDDR applications diversify and contract prices continue to rise, memory manufacturers posted record-high revenue in the first quarter, supported by strong LPDDR sales. Market-research firm TrendForce said, “Mobile DRAM revenue increased by 64.5% in the first quarter of this year,” adding that “continued increases in contract prices will drive further growth in mobile DRAM revenue in the second quarter.”

Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are also seen as having seized the initiative by beginning preparations for mass production of the latest LPDDR6 products ahead of Micron. In January, Samsung unveiled what it described as the industry’s first LPDDR6 product built using fifth-generation 10nm-class (1b) DRAM technology. The product won a CES Innovation Award.

SK hynix’s mass production of LPDDR6 is also expected to signal the start of a full-fledged race to secure an early lead in the SOCAMM market. SOCAMM packages LPDDR into a module designed for AI servers. As the AI market shifts from training toward inference, it is rapidly emerging as a next-generation memory solution for AI servers.

In June, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang visited SK hynix’s booth at Computex 2026, Asia’s largest information-technology trade show, and left the message “LOVE SOCAMM” on a 192GB SOCAMM module.

Nvidia also recently unveiled Vera, its first internally designed CPU for AI servers. If HBM is the GPU’s natural partner, LPDDR is the CPU’s. As the AI market becomes increasingly advanced and demand for CPUs rises sharply, demand for SOCAMM is also expected to strengthen.
— Jukan (@jukan05) Jul 28, 2026
